webTitle: Georgia senator Jon Ossoff slams racist posts allegedly from Republican opponent’s ex-staffer

fields.headline: Georgia senator Jon Ossoff slams racist posts allegedly from Republican opponent’s ex-staffer
fields.trailText: Representative Mike Collins has been dogged by associations to white nationalism and antisemitism
fields.bodyText: The US senator for Georgia Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, has slammed a “disgraceful and disqualifying” report that a former staffer for his Trump-backed Republican challenger Mike Collins shared images online of a swastika and depicting himself in Ku Klux Klan robes. It is the latest instance of someone in Collins’s orbit facing scrutiny over racist or white nationalist conduct. Ossoff called the report “stunning” and said it “should shock the conscience of every Georgian”. The report “confirmed yet more extensive ties between Congressman Mike Collins and white nationalism, and Congressman Mike Collins and neo-Nazi ideology”, said Ossoff. “Mike Collins needs to hold a press conference this afternoon, and he needs to release all the communications between his office and these white supremacists.” Meyer Siegfried, a spokesperson for Collins, said: “Preston Parra has no affiliation with Mike Collins’ office or campaign. The posts are vile, completely unhinged, and Mike Collins unequivocally condemns them.” Siegfried also attempted to highlight other cases of extremism, claiming there had been a “rise in antisemitism and hate among younger Americans” and “Jon Ossoff’s allies”, and describing this as “equally abhorrent”. On Thursday, the Washington Post reported that an ex-staffer for Collins, Preston Parra, who has described himself as a “twink fascist” on his X account, shared images in June and July of a swastika and one that depicts himself in Ku Klux Klan robes. The posts are still there, along with others in which Parra repeatedly casually uses the N-word, quotes Nazi song lyrics and uses the phrase “White Power”. Reached for comment, Parra responded with a racial slur. According to the Post, Parra, 24, interned for Collins for two months in 2024 before working as a contractor for his leadership political action committee the next year. He was paid $7,700 for fundraising consulting in May 2025, according to Federal Election Commission filings, and in an interview with the Post said he worked for the group for several months, shortly before Collins announced his US Senate bid. Responding to the Post’s reporting, Parra told the paper that many of his posts – including the KKK one, which he said he made using Grok AI – were “satirical”. He also said he was not a white supremacist, but added: “I do think that the white race contributes more to the world.” According to Parra, Collins was not aware of Parra’s personal X account when he worked for him because he had made it private. It is just the latest episode in an ever-growing scandal that has embroiled Collins’s bid in the high-stakes Georgia race, which will be critical to control of the Senate. Last month, CNN revealed that Collins’s son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, is a white nationalist and social media influencer with a history of sharing antisemitic material and sentiment and Nazi imagery on the internet. Among them are posts from the neofascist, white supremacist hate group Patriot Front, which descended on Washington DC this Fourth of July wearing white masks and brandishing the Confederate flag. Scheer is registered to vote at a Collins-owned property in Georgia, has been featured in Collins’s campaign photos and was at Collins’s victory party after the candidate won the Republican primary in June, according to CNN’s report. Collins, a trucking executive, has been the GOP representative for Georgia’s 10th congressional district since 2023. In that time he has been plagued by a string of such controversies, drawing scrutiny over his associations with far-right and extremist figures, incendiary social media activity and accusations of antisemitism, which he has denied. Having won the Republican nomination in June, Collins faces rising Democratic star Ossoff in November’s midterm elections. Several Georgia Republicans told the Post that they were increasingly worried about what they see as a pattern of troubling associations and behavior from Collins. “In the south, we have a saying: You lay down with dogs, you get up with fleas,” Debbie Dooley, a prominent conservative activist in Georgia and one of the original Tea Party founders who backed Collins’s rival in the primary, told the paper. “Well, Mike Collins has got a lot of fleas on him.”

webTitle: US Postal Service says new mail ballot rules tied to Trump order are in effect

fields.headline: US Postal Service says new mail ballot rules tied to Trump order are in effect
fields.trailText: Move from USPS comes amid Trump administration’s efforts to restrict mail-in voting in November’s midterms
fields.bodyText: The US Postal Service (USPS) said on Thursday ‌that ‌new ‌requirements for mail-in ‌voting are now ⁠in effect as Donald Trump seeks to crack down on the practice. The move is expected to trigger a new round of legal challenges. The Trump administration has sought to impose new rules requiring state election leaders to submit their voter rolls for inspection as part of a broader bid to increase federal government oversight over voting and elections. The post office requirements stem from an executive order issued by Trump earlier this year, requiring the post office to refrain from delivering ballots for mail-in voting to registered voters deemed ineligible when compared to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other federal records. The USPS posted a final rule on ballot delivery on Friday. On Thursday, the service said it would be implemented immediately, applying to ballots for November’s US midterm elections. The US supreme court ruled on Monday that an injunction by a lower court should be lifted, at least until the post office had begun implementing the rule. The procedural ruling did not address the legality, or constitutionality, of the rule. The constitution confers control over elections to states and Congress, not the executive. US district judge Indira Talwani on Wednesday then lifted her nationwide block on the implementation of the postal service change, citing the supreme court’s decision. Two dozen states and the District of Columbia filed a fresh lawsuit on Wednesday to block the executive order restricting mail voting in this year’s midterm elections. The states said that the USPS policy is part of “a broader effort” by the administration “to rewrite federal election law and usurp the authority of the states and Congress”.

webTitle: Unlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understands | John Crace

fields.headline: Unlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understands
fields.trailText: Burnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respect
fields.bodyText: It makes a pleasant change. Not so long ago, Keir Starmer was falling over himself in his efforts to keep things sweet with Donald Trump. Offering the US president a second state visit within minutes of meeting him. Everyone knows you should never put out on the first date: it only makes the other person think you’re a pushover. Sure enough, The Donald banked the marching bands and the Windsor silver service, made polite conversation for three days and then went back to trash-talking him. Yet still, Starmer just sat there and took it. As if one word of criticism would be too much. Wittering on about the “special relationship” as if Trump gave a moment’s thought to the UK before he did anything. The rest of us wouldn’t have put money on the US president even being able to locate Britain on a map. It was only latterly, when The Donald chose to bomb Iran, that the penny finally dropped for Keir. And even then he looked pained by the apparent betrayal, as he resisted the calls of Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage to join in the war. No such misgivings for Andy Burnham. This week, the prime minister was reminded that when he had been mayor of Greater Manchester, he had said The Donald wouldn’t be welcome in his city and that he could take his poisonous politics elsewhere. Words that had been loudly cheered at the time by many in Britain who had had enough of all the toadying. After all, it wasn’t as if the Trump-whispering had made any difference. If anything, it had only added to his contempt for us. You’ll never get any thanks from a narcissist. Nor did Andy have any regrets now that he was prime minister and was likely to meet Trump in person for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York at the end of next month. Far from it. “Shit happens” was pretty much his precis of what had gone down. He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word. This was the real world. Politicians say stuff. Trump had said all sorts of things about him, too. That he had been mayor of “some town”. To be fair to Agent Orange, it’s quite likely he had never heard of Manchester before. Neither geography nor an interest in other people have ever been his strongest suits. All he had known about Andy was that he was “extremely liberal”. Which in Maga language is the same as saying he’s a “Commy bastard”. So here was Burnham’s deal. He wasn’t planning to go out of his way to insult the US president, but neither would he be offering unexpurgated sycophancy. Instead, we would be getting a very British type of pragmatism. He would do what was necessary in the UK’s interest but not much more. They would be polite and try not to accentuate their differences, but there would be no pretence of any lasting friendship. Just stick to the matters in hand and get the hell out. After New York, Andy wouldn’t be sending weekly WhatsApps. Out of sight, out of mind. Weirdly, this performative show of an ersatz friendship – the US and UK are meant to be more or less on the same side, after all – is likely to be far more effective than Keir’s more needy approach. Because this is the type of language The Donald understands. Although he craves the fawning, he has no respect for those who offer it. He takes it as a sign of weakness. Equally, no amount of flattery is ever enough. There is a hole in Trump’s psyche that can never be filled. With Burnham, there is going to be more a meeting of equals. Two world leaders who are doing what it takes to get along with each other. It’s as close to respect as a sociopath like Trump can get. Andy hasn’t taken a backward step, or attempted to deny his previous comments. More that that was then and this was now. Just get used to it. You can say one thing one day and the opposite the next. It’s up to the other person to work out which one was the truth. Or maybe neither, or maybe both. After all, that’s precisely what The Donald does. Contradiction is his modus operandi. And it’s got him to the White House. So if it works for Trump, why not for Burnham? Sincerity can be an overrated virtue for a world leader. You don’t always need a Love, Actually moment to make your feelings known. “So I’m looking forward, actually, to my first meeting [with Trump],” said Andy. And he probably is. His cards are on the table and he has nothing to hide. Plus, he has a sense of humour and self-deprecation, which also might confuse the US president, who has neither. It also feels as if there’s less at stake with this meeting than there was with many of Starmer’s. Back in the early days of Trump’s presidency, it was as if much of the world was holding its breath for what he might do next. Now, not so much. We’ve all learned to adapt to The Donald. Even to his never-ending war with Iran, which has jacked up the cost of living. All his bad habits are now priced in. And suddenly he looks more vulnerable. A man who has found the world doesn’t automatically bend to his will. A man who is under pressure on the domestic front, with many Americans fed up with his foreign wars and angry at the cost of petrol (never get between an American and their car). A president facing tricky midterm elections and in danger of becoming a lame duck. For Burnham, it’s also the home front that is occupying most of his attention. Good vibes are a decent start, but sooner or later he has to do something different to Starmer while boxing himself in with the same fiscal rules. So who knows? The meeting between Andy and The Donald may be less tricky than first imagined. A welcome distraction for both of them.

webTitle: In a Pennsylvania congressional swing district, a Republican incumbent faces allegations over embellishing résumé

fields.headline: In a Pennsylvania congressional swing district, a Republican incumbent faces allegations over embellishing résumé
fields.trailText: Ryan Mackenzie, running for re-election, is accused of ‘fabricating’ a career in the real estate industry
fields.bodyText: The Republican congressman Ryan Mackenzie has been accused of embellishing his résumé with private sector experience in real estate sales amid an acrimonious showdown over his Pennsylvania seat. Mackenzie, who has previously been accused of lying about his age on Tinder, “was a real estate salesperson licensed in PA”, according to his LinkedIn profile, and biographies have consistently listed it has his former profession. In a statement to the Guardian, however, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) accused the congressman of having “fabricated a career … that never existed”. His campaign would not comment on whether he ever used his real estate license, or made any sales. His office also did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the Tinder allegations, or reports of a staffer scrubbing the story from Wikipedia. Mackenzie is attempting to keep his seat in a Pennsylvania’s seventh congressional district, where he won his first term in 2024 by 1% of the vote. Trump won Pennsylvania in the US presidential election two years ago, after losing the state to Joe Biden in 2020. Mackenzie is running for his seat against Democrat Bob Brooks, former president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association – and has called his opponent a “fraud”, a “conman”, a “lobbyist”, a “dumpster fire candidate” and a “union boss”. Mackenzie’s campaign manager claimed Brooks has “all the hallmarks of a common criminal”. Ahead of the US midterm election in the battleground district, the DCCC has characterized Mackenzie as a career politician who has supported both Trump and policies pursued by the Trump administration that have resulted in increased costs for Americans – including tariffs and the war in Iran. As Mackenzie attacks Brooks, the DCCC has alleged Mackenzie has embellished his résumé, and pointed to misleading citations of “licensed real estate sales”. Mackenzie’s state representative campaign told Patch.com in 2012 he had “private sector experience as a real estate salesperson”. Mackenzie has cited holding a real estate license, which he received in 2006 in Pennsylvania, but did not renew when it expired in 2008. During this same period, he worked for the Republican Federal Committee of Pennsylvania and the US Department of Labor. “Ryan Mackenzie was already disgustingly caught lying about his age on his Tinder profile by nearly 10 years. Now it looks like Mackenzie and his allies have embellished his résumé and fabricated a career in real estate that never existed,” said Eli Cousin, a DCCC spokesperson, in a statement. “The truth is that Mackenzie is a career politician who has seemingly never worked a day in his life outside of politics and straight up does not understand the challenges that working Pennsylvanians are facing.” In 2024, it emerged that Mackenzie had claimed on his Tinder dating profile in 2020 that he was 29 years old when he was actually 37. His office did not deny the allegations at the time. For a 2025 Harvard Business School talk featuring the congressman, Mackenzie would “reflect on his career path from the real estate sector to public service at both the state and federal level”, according to the event’s web listing. A LinkedIn post for the event stated “discussions ranged from how Rep Mackenzie transitioned to and built a career in politics”. Harvard Business School did not respond to multiple requests for comment. A 2025 voter guide by Boeing’s political action committee stated: “Mackenzie worked in real estate.” In Mackenzie’s Pennsylvania state house biography, as part of his professional career history, he cites “licensed real estate sales”. “I was an employee at the US Department of Labor and also I used to hold my real estate salesperson’s license,” Mackenzie told a local Pennsylvania news outlet in 2012 while recounting his job experience. His congressional representative webpage bio cites the license, stating: “He worked on a number of political campaigns and earned his real estate sales license before entering public service.” A spokesperson for Mackenzie, Arnaud Armstrong, would not comment on whether Mackenzie ever used his real estate license or made any sales, and dismissed the touting of the credential as a career profession as “passing mentions, mostly from third parties”.

webTitle: Democratic states sue to block postal service from carrying out Trump’s mail-in voting order – as it happened

fields.headline: Democratic states sue to block postal service from carrying out Trump’s mail-in voting order – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Two dozen mainly Democratic‑led states filed a fresh lawsuit to block Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail voting in this year’s midterm elections. Lawyers for Lisa Cook wrote to the White House on Wednesday, rejecting a new attempt to force the Federal Reserve governor to resign for allegedly listing two properties as her primary residence on mortgage applications. The letter goes on to detail the numerous other individuals who have made the same mistake on mortgage forms, starting with Trump. The chief spokesperson for the US Secret Service and two other communications staffers are under investigation for “potential misconduct” and have been suspended, according to the agency and media reports. A geography professor alleges in a lawsuit filed this week in federal court in Manhattan that he was fired from his tenured position at the US Military Academy at West Point “because he taught that humans influenced climate change”. The US army announced on Wednesday that it has awarded to $2.2bn to five contractors “to own, construct and operate nuclear microreactors on military installations” in five states. A geography professor alleges in a lawsuit filed this week in federal court in Manhattan that he was fired from his tenured position at the US Military Academy at West Point “because he taught that humans influenced climate change” and then protested an order “that this not be mentioned in his classes” as unethical. As first reported by Stars and Stripes, a US government-funded news outlet that cover the US military, the geographer, Adam Kalkstein, says in the suit that he was rated as an “outstanding” professor during his 17 years as a civilian employee teaching climatology to future army officers. According to the complaint, Kalkstein says he was called into on 11 September 2025 by Joel Radunzel, a lieutenant colonel who directs the geography program at West Point. Radunzel, the complaint says, “relayed a verbal order that professors could no longer teach about anthropogenic (human-caused) climate change and that professors must remove all mention of human causes of climate change from their courses.” During the same meeting, Radunzel also issued “a clear threat” that if anyone in the department went to the media or politicians over the ban, “the entire department would likely be dissolved.” “At the time, plaintiff was teaching two sections of Climatology in which he taught that humans were responsible for much of the current planetary warming trend and presented the scientific evidence, consequences, and military impacts,” the complaint explained. “Learning how humans affect the atmosphere was a fundamental component of his course which he had been teaching for many years, and the concept that humans can alter Earth’s climate is a plainly established scientific fact.” Two months later, Kalkstein said he confronted the dean of West Point’s academic board over how hard it was to teach in line with the directive. “I just got out of Climatology class and it’s a struggle” he recalled, “because we’re leaving our essential information. We’re only telling cadets part of the story. We’re lying to them, deceiving them. It would be like trying to teach the law without being able to even mention the Constitution. The guiding principle of any school should be to the truth ... I’m supposed to be an educator and a scientist upholding Army values, but sir, right now, I’m a liar and a fraud. What we’re doing here is wrong. It’s immoral. It’s likely illegal”. The Dean responded angrily, according to the complaint. A US sailor who jumped overboard from the USS Abraham Lincoln this month amid a protracted deployment at sea has been charged by the navy with harming himself to avoid duty and being absent without leave, according to his wife and charging documents reviewed by the broadcaster MS NOW. The sailor and his wife are both 19 years old, MS NOW reports, without revealing their identities. According to the sailor’s wife, although he jumped off the ship in a suicide attempt, he has now been charged with violating two articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice. The broadcaster reports: The charging documents, which were reviewed by MS NOW, show that the sailor has been accused of violating Article 83 for “malingering,” which is defined as a service member “intentionally faking an illness or hurting themselves to avoid work, duty or service,” and Article 86 for “absence without leave,” which means a service member failed to be at their required place of duty without proper authority. “I think they’re insane for doing this to people who need mental help,” the wife told MS NOW. “Instead of giving them help, this is just another huge stressor.” Lawyers for Lisa Cook wrote to the White House on Wednesday, rejecting a new attempt to force the Federal Reserve governor to resign for allegedly listing two properties as her primary residence on mortgage applications. “Governor Cook has never committed mortgage fraud or any intentional wrongdoing, and there is no legally cognizable cause for removing her from the Federal Reserve Board,” her lawyer, Abbe Lowell, wrote to in a letter to the White House Counsel, David Warrington. Lowell cites the opinion of an expert in mortgage regulation and finance who argues that the Trump administration has failed to establish any intentional wrongdoing by Cook, “or that she benefited from the classification of either property as a ‘primary’ residence.” The letter goes on to detail the numerous other individuals who have made the same mistake on mortgage forms, starting with Donald Trump. The President should know firsthand that listing two properties as a ‘primary’ residence does not show intentional wrongdoing or demonstrate ‘unfit[ness] for office’. In 1993, President Trump reportedly acquired ‘primary’ residence mortgages for two different Florida homes just seven weeks apart. For each home, President Trump apparently signed a form attesting that he would occupy the property as his principal residence within 60 days and live there for at least a year. In reality, however, neither property was President Trump’s primary residence. He lived in New York and reportedly listed both Florida properties for rent.10 Surely the President does not believe himself ‘unfit for office’ because he signed these contradictory ‘primary’ mortgage documents. Five current or former members of Trump’s cabinet have reportedly signed the same sort of mortgage application forms, Cook’s lawyer adds: Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary: Todd Blanche, the attorney general; Sean Duffy, the transport secretary and reality TV actor; Lee Zeldin, the EPA administrator; and Lori Chavez-DeRemer, the former labor secretary. Lowell and his co-counsel, Norm Eisen, a former ethics adviser to the Obama administration, said in a statement: “For the second time in a year, we have explained why there is no legal basis for President Trump to remove Governor Cook for cause. An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing. These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will. Our response should put this matter to rest once and for all, but, if necessary and in keeping with the Supreme Court’s ruling, we are prepared to challenge any illegal attempt to remove Governor Cook.” Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the central bank’s board, was appointed by then president Joe Biden in 2022 to a term that lasts until 2038. Trump first tried to fire her last year, in a case that ended with the 5-4 US supreme court ruling, this summer, that the president ‌does not have the authority to remove a Federal Reserve governor without cause. Despite that loss at the nation’s highest court, Trump’s former golf caddy and social media adviser, Dan Scavino, now White House deputy chief of staff, wrote to Cook earlier this month to demand that she reply by Wednesday to a letter laying out the case for her removal. Cook, who has called the administration’s effort to force her out a pretext to gain more power over interest rates, remains on the board. Reuters contributed reporting Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America after not renewing her membership for seven years, amid speculation that she might run for president in 2028. The 36-year-old New York representative and one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists renewed her membership in the group’s national organization after reports emerged earlier this month that it had lapsed. Ocasio-Cortez initially joined the group in 2018. In a statement on Tuesday night, the DSA announced: “Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026,” according to a report in City & State New York. It added: “Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA’s national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month.” The DSA said it decided to disclose Ocasio-Cortez’s membership details amid reports that she could run for president in the next election cycle. Interest in the congresswoman’s status comes as the organization has seen its ranks grow exponentially across the country, following a string of election victories from New York to Florida. “While it is atypical for DSA to address the membership status of individuals, ongoing discussions about the 2028 presidential campaign have prompted this release … With chapters and members campaigning to draft Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as a potential Presidential Primary candidate, we believe that the status of her membership is essential information for members to have in their deliberations and discussions,” the statement said, City & State New York reported. The chief spokesperson for the US Secret Service and two other communications staffers are under investigation for “potential misconduct” and have been suspended, according to the agency and media reports. The spokesperson, Anthony Guglielmi, “is cooperating fully” withe the investigation, his lawyer told CNN, which first reported the news. “Three non-law enforcement personnel at the US Secret Service have been placed on administrative leave pending an investigation into potential misconduct,” the agency said in a statement. “Per policy, this incident is being investigated by the Office of Professional Responsibility. We are unable to comment further at this time.” The investigation comes amid an FBI leak inquiry into how the New York Times discovered that the Secret Service had raised concerns over Donald Trump using a Qatari-gifted luxury jet without the same security capabilities as older Air Force One jets to travel to Turkey for a Nato summit last month. As a result of those concerns, the Washington Post reported, Trump was secretly flown out of the country on a military plane, and an older Air Force One was used as a decoy, amid a supposed plot by Turkey’s neighbor, Iran, to kill the president. Guglielmi, a former chief spokesperson for the Baltimore and Chicago police departments, is being represented by Gregg Bernstein, Baltimore’s former chief prosecutor. In Oregon, which was the first US state to conduct fully vote-by-mail elections, governor Tina Kotek has released a statement of support for the lawsuit filed in federal court by the state’s attorney general, Dan Rayfield, seeking to block the US Postal Sertvuice with implementing Donald Trump’s executive order to restrict mail voting. Kotek said: “The U.S. Constitution gives power to the states to run elections. In Oregon, we uplift the right to vote and have worked hard to strengthen and expand our system to ensure everyone has a voice and that every election is safe and secure. I stand in strong support of Attorney General Rayfield’s fight against President Trump’s unconstitutional, undemocratic attempt to silence people’s voices. We’re doing everything in our power to protect Oregonians’ right to vote.” The US army announced on Wednesday that it has awarded to $2.2bn to five contractors “to own, construct and operate nuclear microreactors on military installations” in five states. “Awarding these contracts accelerates our ability to deliver safe, reliable baseload power directly to our installations,” the army secretary, Dan Driscoll, said. “We are building the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids.” The Pentagon statement said that it “expects more than 20 total nuclear microreactors will be built and operated” on US military installations as part of the project it calls the Janus Program, including additional private sector funding. The selected companies and bases are: Antares Nuclear at Fort Bragg in North Carolina; BWX Technologies at Fort Campbell in Kentucky; General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems at Fort Hood in Texas; Radiant Industries at Fort Benning in Georgia; and Westinghouse Government Services at Fort Drum in New York. The project is part of a Trump administration’s push to incentivize nuclear power, which includes billions in loans for large nuclear reactors to meet increased power demand from AI datacenters and a pilot program to boost advanced reactor designs and projects for military and civilian use. No such nuclear microreactors are supplying power to the commercial electric grid in the United States today. During the Biden administration, the US Department of Energy published an explanatory article, headlined What is a Nuclear Microreactor?, which outlines three key features: Factory fabricated: All components of a microreactor would be fully assembled in a factory and shipped out to location. This eliminates difficulties associated with large-scale construction, reduces capital costs and would help get the reactor up and running quickly. Transportable: Smaller unit designs will make microreactors very transportable. This would make it easy for vendors to ship the entire reactor by truck, shipping vessel, airplane or railcar. Self-adjusting: Simple and responsive design concepts will allow microreactors to self-adjust. They won’t require a large number of specialized operators and would utilize passive safety systems that prevent any potential for overheating or reactor meltdown. The Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization, criticized the appointments of three pro-Israel House Democrats to the foreign affairs committee. As we reported earlier, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, a representative from Florida, and the Missouri representative Wesley Bell will join the committee, while Jared Moskowitz, also from Florida, becomes the Democrats’ ranking member on the subcommittee for the Middle East and north Africa. “We are deeply concerned by the appointment of three of the Israeli government’s most committed and consistent enablers,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, Cair’s deputy director, in a statement. “Members of Congress who want to continue giving the Netanyahu government American taxpayer money knowing it will be used to oppress and kill Palestinian men, women and children are, by definition, anti-Palestinian and out-of-step with the American people.” Several progressives who have been critical of Benjamin Netanyhu’s leadership and the influence of the pro-Israel lobby on recent elections have won their races in recent months – most notably Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic primary in Michigan. Four of the nation’s leading livestock and agricultural organizations have also joined together to urge Donald Trump to reverse the proposed plan to temporarily pause higher tariffs on foreign beef imports, in an attempt to reduce grocery costs for Americans ahead of the midterm elections. “Flooding the market with discounted foreign beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd, strengthen food security, or lower grocery bills in a lasting way,” the groups write in a letter. “This announcement will discourage investment in the US cow herd and undo the progress producers have made.” They add: “We are deeply concerned that this import strategy sacrifices long-term food security for a short-term solution. Americans deserve safe and wholesome beef free from any market distorting actions.” This week, I’ve been reporting on the growing backlash to policy, including from several Republicans in states with sizable cattle industries who have issued rare rebukes of the president’s decision. The federal judge who issued the injunction blocking parts of Donald Trump’s executive order curbing mail-in voting has lifted her block, after the supreme court said on Monday that the challenge from mainly Democratic-led states was premature, saying they lacked standing. However, Judge Indira Talwani said that she would consider further challenges now that the US Postal Service had published its rule outlining how it will refuse to deliver mail-in ballots in states that refuse to give the Department of Homeland Security and other agencies access to lists of voters. As I reported earlier, a coalition of states filed a fresh lawsuit on Wednesday to challenge the USPS policy. And a reminder that the constitution confers control over elections to states and Congress, not the executive. “Congress has not afforded USPS any authority whatsoever to set rules for federal elections or mail voting, even though Americans have cast ballots by mail for generations,” the states argue in the new lawsuit. They also said although the deadline to submit mail voter lists to USPS “is still several weeks away”, the new rule “is already causing acute harm”. “Plaintiff states or their subdivisions must immediately redesign their ballot envelopes and seek USPS review at significant costs to states,” they added. On Truth Social, Donald Trump said that Ralph Norman, the South Carolina representative who lost the Republican primary for Senate to Darline Graham on Tuesday, had “the look” of a good congressman, but “ruined his career when he endorsed Nikki Haley”. Trump backed Graham, after her brother, the late senator Lindsey Graham, died last month. Norman was shunned by the president as the only member of Congress to endorse Haley, the former governor of South Carolina, over Trump in the 2024 election. The race to replace Lindsey Graham on the ballot became a stress test of the president’s support, and how effectively his endorsement can carry a candidate in deep-red pockets of the country to victory. A federal judge has, for a second time, struck down a Texas state law banning drag performances in settings where children may be present. In a ruling issued on Tuesday, the US district judge David Hittner said Texas cannot enforce its drag show ban. He said that the measure improperly restricts speech and violates the first amendment of the US constitution. The Texas ban, known as Senate Bill 12, was passed in March 2023 and bans drag performers from dancing suggestively or wearing certain prosthetics on public property or in front of children, or “sexually oriented performance” presented on the premises in the presence of an individual younger than 18 years of age. Advocacy groups sued the state after the bill’s passage, arguing the ban on “sexually oriented performance” infringed on constitutional rights. Texas’s move was just one across several states in 2023, driven by a rightwing backlash to increasing queer and transgender rights and equality.
